back: One token per forward pass; each token depends on all previous ones, so a reply of N tokens needs N sequential passes.

front: What does the KV cache store?
back: The key and value vectors of every previous token, for every layer and KV head. Queries are not cached.
With a causal mask, the K and V of token i depend only on tokens up to i; appending tokens never changes them.

front: Naive step cost with t tokens
back: $F_\text{naive}(t)=6\,t\,d\,d_h+2\,t(t+1)\,d_h$: projections of all rows plus a causal $t\times t$ attention. Quadratic in t.

front: Cached step cost with t tokens
back: $F_\text{cached}(t)=6\,d\,d_h+4\,t\,d_h$: one token's projections plus one query against t keys. Linear in t.
$2\cdot L\cdot n_{kv}\cdot d_h\cdot T\cdot b\cdot B$ bytes (2 = K and V; b = bytes per number; B = batch).
Prefill: all prompt tokens in parallel, compute-bound, fills the cache. Decode: one token per step, memory-bandwidth-bound.
Each step reads all weights and the whole cache for a single token's worth of arithmetic: very low ops-per-byte.
Groups of query heads share one K/V head, so $n_{kv}=n_\text{heads}/g$ and the cache shrinks by the group size g.
Extreme GQA with a single K/V head shared by all query heads: smallest cache, largest quality risk.

front: Shape of the cache for one layer
back: $K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{t\times d_h}$ per KV head; the full tensor is $(L,2,B,n_{kv},T,d_h)$.

front: How to test a cache implementation
back: Generate with and without it from the same weights and compare outputs: they must agree to rounding error.
The full sequence is available and processed in parallel with a causal mask; there is no step-by-step regeneration to save.
Halves (int8) or quarters memory, but errors in K and V influence every later token, so the loss in quality grows with context length.
The memory traffic of attention (tiling, no full score matrix in slow memory); the result is mathematically the same.
